patch.value: The --profile timer reports a fraction of real invocation latency and is documented nowhere, so every latency judgement built on it is calibrated against the wrong number

pm exposes a global --profile flag described in root help as 'Print deterministic timing diagnostics'. Fifty-eight call sites emit a single line, profile:command=<name> took_ms=<n>, computed as Date.now() minus a start timestamp taken inside the command handler. That span excludes process start, module graph resolution, settings and schema load, extension loading, and output rendering, which together are the majority of what a caller actually waits for.

Measured on this repository's live tracker (2,037 items), dist build 2026.7.25, wall clock from the shell against the number the same invocation printed:

  pm list --limit 5              wall 1004 ms   profile 200 ms    20 percent reported
  pm get pm-doxj                 wall  882 ms   profile 286 ms    32 percent
  pm graph audit                 wall 1470 ms   profile 521 ms    35 percent
  pm next --limit 3              wall 1307 ms   profile 577 ms    44 percent
  pm search context --limit 5    wall 1539 ms   profile 602 ms    39 percent
  pm context --limit 5           wall 1410 ms   profile 684 ms    49 percent
  pm stats                       wall 1887 ms   profile 1155 ms   61 percent
  pm validate                    wall 8135 ms   profile 7200 ms   89 percent

The un-instrumented remainder is roughly 600 to 800 ms and is close to constant, so the instrument is least truthful exactly where the product most wants to be fast. On pm list it hides four fifths of the cost. An agent or maintainer using --profile to decide whether a command is fast reads 200 ms for a one-second wait, and any budget or ratchet built on the printed value would pass while the experienced latency regressed.

Second half: --profile appears in no file under docs/. It is a global flag on every command with no reference documentation, no statement of what span it measures, and no note that the number is not end-to-end. There is nothing to correct the natural reading of took_ms as total command time.

Scope boundary. pm-yse5dt owns the per-invocation bootstrap floor and the CLI-versus-SDK delta as gated metrics; pm-801d owns read scaling; pm-9rxu owns the scale program. This item is about the measuring instrument rather than the thing measured: those items need a truthful timer to gate against, and today the only built-in one systematically under-reports.

The --profile output reports end-to-end invocation latency measured from process entry to output flush, and any narrower spans it also reports are labelled with what they cover so the total and its parts are distinguishable. The reported total agrees with externally measured wall clock within a stated tolerance for every command family, asserted by a regression test rather than by inspection. --profile is documented with its measured span and its output shape. Any latency budget or ratchet in this repository consumes the end-to-end figure.

author: harness:claude-code
message: Strategic reachability edge: mirror the hierarchy rung into the typed layer so every active item resolves to an outcome milestone through an explainable implements path (pm-bzmeaa invariant), which the parent chain alone cannot express because it terminates at the roadmap root rather than at an outcome

value.author: harness:opencode
value.text: Fresh evidence 2026-07-26 (audit plan pm-t9e3bc): wall-clock re-measured on live tracker now at 2,066 items, dist 2026.7.26, Node 25.9.0 — pm context --limit 5: 1132/1224/1306ms across runs; pm search audit --limit 5: 1005/1105/1151ms; pm list-open --limit 5: 743/919ms; pm get pm-doxj --depth brief: 635/875ms; pm --version: 57ms; pm contracts --flags-only: 643ms. The ~600-800ms constant un-instrumented floor this item documents persists unchanged on current main; experienced read latency at the 2k-item dogfood scale remains ~1s+ for context/search, so the pm-801d read index relieves daily agent-perceived latency long before the 100k-item scale framing.
